stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Sweep the density $\rho$ and depth $h$ sliders. Watch how the pressure gauge on the probe changes. Advance when each slider has covered at least half its range.
stages.concept: Hydrostatic pressure at depth $h$ in a liquid of density $\rho$: $p(h) = p_0 + \rho\,g\,h$. Here $p_0 = 100\,\text{kPa}$ (atmospheric) and $g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2$. Pressure grows linearly with depth, and the slope $\rho g$ depends only on the liquid — the tank shape does not enter.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: A target pressure $p^*$ is shown at the top. Choose a liquid (density) and a probe depth so that the probe reads $p^*$ within $\pm 3\%$.
stages.concept: Many pairs $(\rho, h)$ can satisfy $p_0 + \rho g h = p^*$. Pick a liquid first, then solve $h = (p^* - p_0) / (\rho g)$ for the required depth. If your depth falls outside the tank, try a denser (or less dense) liquid.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: The pressure gauge and colour gradient are hidden. Only the target pressure $p^*$ remains. Compute the depth on paper for your chosen liquid, then set the sliders and submit. One try per setup.
stages.concept: Rearrange the formula: $h^* = (p^* - p_0) / (\rho\,g)$. Convert $p^*$ from kPa to Pa first (multiply by $1000$). Pick a liquid whose $\rho$ makes $h^*$ land inside the tank ($0 \le h \le 20\,\text{m}$).

labels.tip1: sweep both sliders to at least half their range
labels.tip2: pick a liquid first, then choose a depth so the gauge reads p*
labels.tip3: compute h = (p* − p₀) / (ρ·g) on paper before touching the sliders
labels.peek_tip_formula: Rearrange: h* = (p* − p₀) / (ρ·g). Convert p* to Pa (×1000). Pick ρ so h* fits in 0..20 m.
labels.peek_tip_anchor: Anchor: water (ρ=1000) at h=10 m gives p = 200 kPa. Denser liquid → shallower depth.

1.1: Move each slider from one end to the other. Watch the probe gauge.
1.2: Density controls the slope of the pressure vs. depth line. Depth moves you along that line.
1.3: The pressure gauge shows p = p₀ + ρ·g·h. At h = 0 you read p₀ regardless of ρ.

2.1: Read the target pressure p* at the top. It is the total pressure, not the excess.
2.2: Subtract atmospheric: ρ·g·h = p* − p₀. Now pick any ρ and solve for h.
2.3: For example, if p* = 200 kPa, you need ρ·g·h = 100 kPa = 100000 Pa. Water (ρ=1000, g=10) gives h = 10 m.

3.1: The gauge is off, but the formula still holds. Write it on paper.
3.2: h* = (p* − p₀) / (ρ·g). Pick a liquid whose ρ puts h* between 0 and 20 m.
3.3: Convert p* from kPa to Pa first (multiply by 1000). Then divide by (ρ·g) — with g = 10 that is just ρ·10.
